title: 10 Tips for Dealing with Exam Stress & Looking After your Mental Health
context: Exam periods can bring pressure around grades, deadlines, family expectations, and what comes next after school. This student-led video shares practical ideas for looking after yourself when revision and exams feel overwhelming. It was created in the UK, so do not rely on any helpline or service details mentioned; use MindBridge’s Nigeria-specific support options if you need further help.

title: Exam stress – for 11-18 year olds
context: This resource explains common ways exam pressure can affect your thoughts, mood, body, sleep, and behaviour. Although it was written in the UK for younger students, the signs of feeling overwhelmed by tests, deadlines, grades, or academic expectations can still be useful for Nigerian university students. Use it to reflect on what you are experiencing, not to diagnose yourself

title: Tips to help with exam stress
context: This resource offers small, practical ways to cope when exams, deadlines, and revision are making you feel overwhelmed. Some school and support examples come from the UK, but strategies such as taking realistic breaks, planning manageable tasks, protecting sleep, and talking to someone you trust can still be useful.

title: Exam Self-Care
context: This student-focused article is about making space for rest, balance, and kindness toward yourself when exam pressure is high. It was written in the UK, but the experience of feeling overwhelmed by revision, grades, or expectations can be familiar anywhere. Take what fits your situation and leave any suggestion that is not realistic for you right now.

title: How to manage exam stress
context: This resource focuses on practical ways to handle exam pressure, such as breaking tasks into smaller steps and planning rest alongside study. It was created for UK school examinations, so the exam system and support services may differ from your university experience in Nigeria. The study-planning and stress-management ideas can still help when coursework or tests feel like too much.

title: What is stress?
context: This resource explains how stress can affect your body, thoughts, mood, sleep, and behaviour, and suggests practical ways to cope. It was created by the UK National Health Service, so its therapy and emergency contact details are not for Nigeria. The stress-management ideas can still help you reflect on what is affecting you and choose one small next step.

title: How to manage stress and build resilience
context: This resource can help you notice what is contributing to your stress and choose realistic ways to respond, such as breaking tasks into smaller steps, taking breaks, and asking for support. It also recognizes that money worries, loneliness, difficult living conditions, and limited access to services can make stress harder to manage—and that this is not your fault. Some services and examples are UK-based, but the reflection and coping ideas can still be useful.

title: What is Anxiety?
context: This short video explains the difference between ordinary nervousness and anxiety that begins to interfere with school, relationships, sleep, or daily life. It can help you put words to what you are feeling, but it cannot diagnose you. The emergency contacts mentioned in the video are for the United States, so use MindBridge’s Nigeria-specific support options if you need urgent help.

title: Anxiety Disorders
context: This resource explains how anxiety can affect thoughts, sleep, concentration, the body, relationships, and daily life. It can help you understand why persistent worry, panic-like feelings, avoidance, or fear of judgment may be difficult to manage, but it cannot diagnose you. The treatment and crisis information comes from the United States, so use MindBridge’s Nigeria-specific support options if anxiety is seriously affecting your studies, safety, or ability to cope.

title: Self-help CBT techniques
context: This resource shares practical ways to handle worry, difficult thoughts, avoidance, and overwhelming to-do lists. It uses ideas from cognitive behavioural therapy, but you do not need to know any clinical terms to try the exercises. It was created in the UK, so therapy links may not apply in Nigeria; use the techniques as self-help and seek local support if your distress feels severe or unsafe.

title: Generalised Anxiety and Worry: Worksheets and Workbook
context: This workbook is for people who notice that worry or overthinking keeps returning and affects daily life. It offers step-by-step exercises on uncertainty, attention, problem-solving, and unhelpful worry patterns. It was created in Australia and uses some clinical language, so use it as a self-help learning tool—not as a way to diagnose yourself—and take it one section at a time.

title: Five mindful journaling prompts to tackle anxiety
context: This resource offers short journaling prompts that can help you slow down, notice anxious thoughts, and reflect on what you may need. It was written in the UK, but the prompts can be used anywhere with a notebook or notes app. Journaling is not a replacement for professional support—pause if it makes you feel more overwhelmed, and seek help if anxiety is affecting your safety or daily life.

title: The Cure for Burnout — Hint: It Isn't Self-Care
context: This video may help if you feel emotionally exhausted, disconnected from your work or studies, or worried that you are never doing enough. It explains that burnout is not a sign of weakness and that rest, support, and changes to overwhelming demands can matter. The examples are mostly from the United States and work settings, but the ideas may still be useful for students managing heavy academic, financial, or family pressure.

title: Work-related stress
context: This resource can help if studies, internships, part-time work, job searching, or responsibilities at home are leaving you stressed and drained. It includes practical ideas such as identifying triggers, setting realistic limits, taking short breaks, and talking to someone you trust. It was written in the UK for workers, so NHS support links may not apply in Nigeria, but the coping tools can still be useful.

title: Dealing with burnout when working from home
context: This resource may help if online classes, remote work, freelance work, or studying from home has made it hard to separate work time from rest time. It shares practical ideas about sleep, boundaries, breaks, and asking for support. It was written in the UK for workers, so any helpline details are not Nigeria-specific, but the self-care ideas can still be adapted to your routine.

title: You are not alone in your loneliness | Jonny Sun | TED
context: This talk may help if you feel isolated, like you do not belong, or like no one understands what you are carrying. It reminds us that loneliness is a shared human experience and that small moments of connection can matter. The speaker talks about finding community online, but you do not need to share personal information publicly to seek connection—choose spaces and people that feel safe for you.

title: Social connection
context: This resource explains the difference between being alone, feeling lonely, and feeling disconnected from people around you. It may help you understand why you can feel lonely even when you are on campus, in class, or surrounded by others. It is written for a global audience, but the ideas can still help you reflect on the kinds of connection you need and what small next step may feel safe.

title: What is loneliness?
context: This resource explains why loneliness is not the same as simply being alone. You can have people around you and still feel unseen, unsupported, or disconnected—especially during transitions such as starting university, moving, financial stress, or relationship changes. It was created in the UK, so its helpline details are not for Nigeria, but the information can help you make sense of what you are feeling.

title: How to manage loneliness
context: This resource offers gentle, practical ideas for feeling less alone, such as messaging someone you trust, starting with small social interactions, finding interest-based groups, and reducing unhelpful comparison online. Some examples and support services are from the UK, but you can adapt the ideas to your campus, study group, faith community, student association, or trusted online space. Go at your own pace—you do not have to force yourself into social situations that feel unsafe or overwhelming.

title: From loneliness to social connection: Plain Language Summary
context: This resource explains why loneliness and social disconnection are not personal failures—they can be shaped by money pressures, relocation, exclusion, difficult life changes, and limited access to supportive communities. It is a global WHO report, so it does not give Nigeria-specific support options or quick coping steps. Read it if you want to understand the bigger picture behind loneliness and why connection matters.

title: I had a black dog, his name was depression
context: This short animated video uses a “black dog” as a metaphor for how depression can affect energy, concentration, enjoyment, relationships, and hope. It may help you find words for experiences that are hard to explain, but it cannot diagnose you. The story was created outside Nigeria, and the coping ideas may not work the same way for everyone—if you feel unsafe, unable to cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself, use MindBridge’s urgent-support options.

title: Depressive disorder (depression)
context: This WHO resource explains how depression can affect mood, interest in activities, sleep, concentration, energy, appetite, and hope. It can help you understand when low mood may be lasting longer or affecting daily life more than ordinary stress, but it cannot diagnose you.

title: Get help with low mood, sadness or depression
context: This resource can help you understand the difference between a temporary low mood and feelings that are lasting longer or affecting your sleep, studies, relationships, or ability to cope. It includes small practical steps such as talking to someone, setting manageable goals, eating regularly, and protecting sleep. It was created in the UK, so its helpline and therapy options may not apply in Nigeria

title: My Mental Health: Do I Need Help?
context: This resource can help you reflect on whether what you are feeling is mild and temporary, becoming harder to manage, or affecting your daily life. It is not a diagnosis and you do not need to wait for a certain number of days before seeking help if you feel unsafe, overwhelmed, or unable to cope. The crisis numbers in the original resource are for the United States, so use MindBridge’s Nigeria-specific support options if you need urgent help.

title: Depression Self-Help Resources
context: This resource contains guided worksheets for low mood, including small activity planning, problem-solving, noticing unhelpful thoughts, and setting manageable goals. It was created in Australia and uses clinical language, so use it as a self-help learning tool—not as a way to diagnose yourself. Start with one short activity, and seek local support if low mood is making it hard to study, care for yourself, or stay safe.

title: Teens: My Self-Care
context: This short video shares simple self-care ideas such as protecting sleep, setting boundaries, staying connected, keeping a routine, and choosing healthier ways to cope with stress. It was made in the United States for teenagers, so take the ideas that fit your life and ignore any that are not realistic for you right now. Self-care is not a cure or a replacement for support when you are struggling to cope.

title: 5 steps to mental wellbeing
context: This resource shares five simple areas that can support wellbeing: connection, movement, learning, kindness, and paying attention to the present moment. You can adapt the ideas to your own life—for example, joining a study group, taking a short walk, learning something small online, or checking in with someone you trust. It is general wellbeing guidance, not treatment, so seek more support if stress or low mood is seriously affecting your daily life.

title: Self-care for mental health problems
context: This resource offers practical ways to care for yourself when you are under emotional pressure, including noticing triggers, tracking mood changes, identifying early warning signs, staying connected, and choosing activities that help you feel steadier. It was created in the UK, so some helplines and organizations mentioned may not be available in Nigeria. Use the ideas that fit your situation, and remember that self-care can support you but does not replace professional help when you need it.

title: What to Expect in Therapy
context: This short video explains what a first therapy session may be like and why it is normal to feel nervous before speaking to someone new. It was created in the United States, so booking processes, professional titles, costs, and crisis contacts may differ in Nigeria. You can still use it to understand that therapy should be collaborative and that it is okay to ask a provider about their training, confidentiality, approach, and fees.

title: Talking therapies
context: This resource explains what talking therapy is and introduces different forms of support, such as counselling, CBT, and one-to-one or online sessions. It was created for the UK National Health Service, so the referral routes and free-service options may not apply in Nigeria. Use it to understand what therapy can involve, then check MindBridge’s Nigeria-specific guidance for local support options.

title: Counselling
context: This resource explains what counselling is and what you might expect if you speak with a trained professional about stress, low mood, worry, relationship challenges, or school pressure. It was created for the UK, so its NHS referral and registration information may not apply in Nigeria. You can still use it to understand that counselling should be non-judgmental, confidential within professional limits, and focused on helping you explore your own next steps.

title: My Mental Health: Do I Need Help?
context: This resource can help you reflect on whether what you are feeling is temporary, becoming harder to manage, or affecting your studies, relationships, sleep, or ability to cope. It is not a diagnosis, and you do not need to wait for a certain number of days before seeking help if you feel unsafe or overwhelmed. The crisis contacts in the original resource are for the United States

title: Lagos Lifeline — 24-hour mental health helpline
context: If you feel overwhelmed, unsafe, are having thoughts of harming yourself, or need someone to talk to right now, Lagos Lifeline says it offers free, confidential support by phone or WhatsApp. You can call 070 0000 6463 or 020 1410 6463, or message 090 9000 6463 on WhatsApp. If there is immediate danger to life, call 112 in Nigeria or go to the nearest emergency service.

title: Mental Health Crisis and Emergency Services
context: Use this resource if something is happening right now and you need urgent help. For immediate danger to life, call 112 anywhere in Nigeria; for emotional crisis or suicidal thoughts, Lagos MiND lists Lagos Lifeline at 070 0000 6463 or 020 1410 6463. Some emergency services on this page are specific to Lagos, so check your location and use the nearest available emergency option.

title: Mental Health Resource Centre
context: This Nigeria-focused resource can help you find information on stress, anxiety, low mood, self-care, self-harm, and where to seek further support. It also lists counselling contacts and mental-health facilities in several states. If you need urgent help, use the emergency section carefully and choose the option that fits your situation; contact details and service availability can change, so MindBridge will show the latest verified options where possible.
